messages.subject: Re: Help interpreting ezANOVA results for mixed designs
messages.subject_clean: Help interpreting ezANOVA results for mixed designs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike and everyone,

Below are the results I speak of. As you can see, this is a five
factor design with all factors within except "display". All effects
related to display are shown twice. In some cases, they are
significant in one line, not significant in another. What does this
mean?

Also, the degrees of freedom do not seem to be related to the levels
of the factors. I am used to seeing such a relationship. I wonder what
I'm doing wrong?

Best,

Ben

***

On May 11, 11:12 pm, Mike Lawrence <Mike.Lawre...@dal.ca> wrote:

> Hi Ben,
>
> When one runs an ANOVA with multiple variables, regardless of whether
> they're within or between, most software will produce multiple rows of
> output corresponding to the tests of the main effects of each variable
> as well as the interactions between the variables (2-way interactions,
> 3-way interactions, etc). In your case, I presume that you're looking
> at the top-most rows of the anova output where the tests of the main
> effects is printed. If, as you suggest, one row shows a "significant"
> effect and the other row doesn't, this means that the former variable
> has a "significant" main effect while the latter variable does not. It
> is important to look further down the rows however, as these main
> effects may be qualified by higher-order interactions between the
> variables.
>
> Mike
>
>
>
>
>
>
>
> On Wed, Apr 20, 2011 at 3:39 PM, Ben Watson <wats...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > I see that in a mixed design with both within and between variables,
> > the effects involving the between variables are shown on two lines.
> > These two lines are not the same, that is they will have different DF,
> > F, p, etc.
>
> > What is the difference between these two lines, and what do the
> > differences between them mean? E.g., if the effect is significant in
> > one case and not in the other, what is the applied meaning?
>
> > Thanks,
>
> > Ben.

>>> as well as the interactions between the variables (2-way interactions,
>>> 3-way interactions, etc). In your case, I presume that you're looking
>>> at the top-most rows of the anova output where the tests of the main
>>> effects is printed. If, as you suggest, one row shows a "significant"

>>> has a "significant" main effect while the latter variable does not. It
>>> is important to look further down the rows however, as these main
>>> effects may be qualified by higher-order interactions between the
